meta.note: All figures provisional and subject to revision by the issuing statistical office.

markets.name: United Kingdom
markets.commentary: Headline jumped to 2.9% from 2.6%, the first rise since March. It is all energy and housing: the housing and household services rate went from 1.2% to 4.6% on gas and electricity, contributing almost the whole change. Core held at 2.6% for a second month and services actually eased to 3.4% from 3.6%, so underlying pressure is not building. Factory gate prices cooled again to 3.1% from 3.5% and input prices dropped to 4.9% from a revised 7.4% as crude oil inputs fell 18.0% in the month. The pipeline is deflating while the shelf price rises, which is the opposite of the pattern that held all spring.

markets.name: Euro Area
markets.commentary: Back up to 2.9% from 2.8%, reversing last month's fall. Energy is the driver again, accelerating to 10.3% year on year from 8.5% and adding 2.7% in the single month. Core (excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) ticked up to 2.5% from 2.4% and services firmed to 3.3%, so this is not purely an energy story any more. Food, alcohol and tobacco kept falling, down to 1.2% from 1.5%, which is holding the headline down. Producer prices for June, the latest published, fell 0.3% on the month and eased to 4.6% year on year from 5.9% in May, so the pipeline is cooling even as consumer energy costs rise.

markets.name: United States
markets.commentary: The cooling continued, but slowly. Headline rose 0.1% on the month after June's 0.4% fall, taking the annual rate down to 3.4% from 3.5%. Core edged up 0.2% on the month yet fell to 2.5% year on year from 2.6%, so the trend is still the right way. Energy fell another 1.5% in the month with gasoline down 2.9%, though the annual energy rate is still 14.7%. PPI final demand was flat on the month and eased to 4.7% year on year from 5.5%, helped by a 3.1% monthly drop in final demand energy. Watch airline fares, up 2.2% in the month and 25.5% over the year, which is now the single most inflationary line in the core basket.

markets.name: Japan
markets.commentary: Third month moving up. Headline reached 1.9%, the highest this year, and the measure excluding fresh food and energy rose to 1.9% from 1.7%. The narrower measure excluding fresh food only went to 1.8% from 1.6%, still under the Bank of Japan's 2% target for a seventh month because fuel subsidies are holding it there. Energy prices rose for the first time since November 2025. CGPI was broadly flat at 7.2% year on year, up 0.1% on the month, with electricity and gas the biggest positive and petroleum and coal products falling 2.7%. Import prices on a yen basis are still 29.1% higher than a year ago. Service sector inflation picked up to 1.2% from 1.1%, the first sign that labour costs are feeding through rather than just import costs. The CPI switched to a 2025 base with this release, so back series have been revised. Monthly CPI rates are not published on a seasonally adjusted basis, hence n/a.

euroMembers.name: Germany
euroMembers.note: The sharpest reversal of the four. HICP went from 2.4% to 2.8% and energy from 3.4% to 8.3% year on year, because the government fuel discount ended on 30 June and oil rose on the Iran conflict at the same time. Motor fuel prices jumped 11.2% in the single month. Core actually fell to 2.4% from 2.5%, so nothing underlying has changed. Producer prices at 1.9% for June are now below consumer prices.

euroMembers.name: France
euroMembers.note: Last month's sharp drop did not hold. HICP back up to 2.4% from 2.0%, with the national CPI at 2.1% after 1.8%. Energy accelerated to 12.6% from 11.0% and services to 2.2% from 1.9%. Core rose to 1.3% from 1.0% but is still the lowest of the four by a wide margin.

euroMembers.name: Italy
euroMembers.note: The only one of the four that eased, down to 2.9% from 3.0%, and core held at 1.6%. The monthly HICP fall of 1.0% is summer sales, not disinflation. Regulated energy is the thing to watch: it went from 9.2% to 14.8% year on year and rose 6.5% in the month, while non regulated energy came down from 13.3% to 11.4%. Producer prices are still the hottest of the four at 6.8% for June, down from 9.1% in May.

euroMembers.name: Spain
euroMembers.note: Still the highest of the four and now rising again. HICP up to 3.9% from 3.6%, national CPI to 3.6% from 3.2%, core up to 3.0%. Transport went to 6.2% on fuel and housing to 5.7% on electricity. Spain has now been at or above 3.6% on the national measure for two months and its core is the highest of the four for a fourth month running.

euroMembersNote: Headline HICP year on year and month on month are both shown on the comparable Eurostat basis (final July 2026 release, published 19 August). Core measures come from each national office and are not identical: Germany is CPI excluding food and energy, France is INSEE underlying inflation, Italy is NIC excluding energy and unprocessed food, Spain is CPI excluding unprocessed food and energy. PPI is held at June 2026 for all four so it stays comparable with the euro area aggregate (+4.6%), which is the latest published month; the July euro area figure is due early September. On that June basis: Germany +1.9%, France +2.6%, Italy +6.8%, Spain +7.0%.

signals.title: Europe and the US have swapped places on energy
signals.observe: Euro area headline went back up to 2.9% from 2.8% with energy at 10.3% year on year, and the UK jumped to 2.9% from 2.6% on gas and electricity. Over the same month the US fell to 3.4% from 3.5% with energy down 1.5% and gasoline down 2.9%. Germany is the clearest case: energy went from 3.4% to 8.3% year on year after the fuel discount ended on 30 June.
signals.why: The US spike in May and its reversal in June were oil price moves that have now washed through. Europe's rise is different. Part is oil, but a bigger part is policy support being withdrawn, the German fuel discount and Italy's regulated energy tariffs going from 9.2% to 14.8%.
signals.action: Do not read the European rise as a demand signal. Core is flat or falling almost everywhere, so this should unwind as the base effects pass. But anything tied to European energy costs in Q3 and Q4 needs modelling off the current rate, not the June low.

signals.title: The UK headline moved but nothing underneath it did
signals.observe: CPI rose 0.3 percentage points to 2.9%, yet core stayed at 2.6% for the second month and services eased to 3.4% from 3.6%. Housing and household services alone went from 1.2% to 4.6%. On the other side, factory gate prices fell again to 3.1% and input prices dropped to 4.9% from a revised 7.4%.
signals.why: The whole move is the energy component of the domestic bill. Producer costs are going the other way, and services inflation, which is the labour cost proxy, is now falling.
signals.action: If the 2.9% print triggers any internal repricing conversation, push back with the core and services numbers. The cost pressure that would actually justify a price change is easing, not building.

signals.title: Japan is the only market where the producer gap is not closing
signals.observe: Japan's CGPI at 7.2% against CPI at 1.9% is a gap of 5.3 percentage points. Everywhere else the gap narrowed this month: US PPI 4.7% against CPI 3.4% is 1.3 points, down from 2.0 last month; euro area 4.6% against 2.9% is 1.7 points, down from 3.1; Germany's producer prices at 1.9% are now below consumer prices.
signals.why: Japanese suppliers are absorbing import costs that are still 29.1% higher year on year on a yen basis, while subsidies hold the shelf price down. Service sector inflation ticking up to 1.2% from 1.1% is the first evidence that pass through has started. Analysts quoted around the release expect core to pass 2% by autumn.
signals.action: Keep pricing Japan linked inputs off the 7.2% CGPI, not the 1.9% CPI, and assume the gap closes upward rather than the producer number falling. Elsewhere the urgency flagged in the last two refreshes can come down; the US and European gaps are back to normal ranges.
